The ShotLoc training model operates under a dual hypothesis: that mechanical guidance reduces variability in kinematic inputs, thereby increasing free throw accuracy. The primary operator 'shotloc_efficacy' quantifies this effect as a net gain in free throw percentage (ΔFT% = +6.6%) versus control group (ΔFT% = -0.6%). This implies a probabilistic shift in the underlying distribution of successful shots. The secondary operator 'kinematic_stability' suggests minimal change in most kinematic variables but significant increase in wrist flexion among controls, indicating that ShotLoc may stabilize other aspects of motion without altering core biomechanics. The third operator 'technique_feedback' posits that tactile input from the device acts as a corrective signal, aligning hand position with optimal release geometry. These primitives form a coherent system where feedback drives convergence toward stable shooting patterns. Failure modes include insufficient feedback strength or misalignment of device with natural movement dynamics. Dualities arise in how mechanical aids can either enhance or constrain motor learning depending on adherence to prescribed form.
